# SK2040 — The comparison is by reference where value equality was meant

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`==` on a source class that defines value equality and declares no `operator ==`, so the comparison is by reference and cannot mean what it says.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

A type that overrides `Equals(object)` has written down what equality means for it, and `==` on that type does not use it: with no `operator ==` anywhere on the chain the comparison falls back to reference identity, so two instances the type itself calls equal compare `false`. It does not fail, which is why it survives review and outlives the test suite.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
// Money overrides Equals(object) and declares no operator ==
if (left == right) { }
```

Write:

```csharp
if (Equals(left, right)) { }
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Only the built-in reference `==` is reported.** An operation that binds to a user-defined operator is never a finding, which excludes records, `string`, `Uri`, `Version` and every type that declares `operator ==` on itself or inherits one from a base — the check is on the bound operator, not on a list of names. Both operands must have the *same* named type, and that type must be a class **declared in this compilation**: a framework type whose `Equals` override the author cannot see is deliberately out of scope, because `encoding == Encoding.UTF8` reads as identity against a cached singleton and calling it wrong needs knowledge of what the library guarantees. `null` and `default` operands are never reported, because a null check is not a value comparison; neither is an operand spelled `this` or `base`. Nothing inside `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `CompareTo` or `operator ==`/`!=` is reported at all — an identity short circuit there is the idiom rather than a mistake. Interfaces, type parameters, delegates, `object` and error types are excluded. ⚠ **`ReferenceEquals` on a value type is not part of this rule, and it was built before it was withdrawn.** A probe compiled against a real project showed `CA2013` reporting exactly that shape, with the same advice, enabled by default — so ADR-008 hosts it rather than Skala restating it, and `ReferenceEqualsWithValueType` is recorded in the hosted map instead of the parity map. ⚠ **Two more inspections in this concept are declined.** `CompareNonConstrainedGenericWithNull` (`t == null` on an unconstrained `T`) is declined because the repair is a constraint or an `EqualityComparer<T>.Default` call rather than an edit to the comparison, and because the export itself ships it at `none`; `CheckForReferenceEqualityInstead` is the mirror direction and asks what the author meant rather than what the code does, which is not decidable from the shape. The fix rewrites the comparison to `Equals(a, b)`, which is null-safe and dispatches to the override; it carries `fixIsSafe: false` because it changes the answer, and changing the answer is the entire point of the finding. ⚠ **A type whose base list did not bind is withdrawn, and that was found by measuring rather than by reading.** On the reference trees a class declaring `IEquatable<Self>` was reported for not implementing it: without the SDK's implicit global usings the name bound to an *error* type, so the interface list held `IEquatable<>` and the comparison against `System.IEquatable`1` failed. Skala loads a compilation three ways and two of them can be incomplete, so an error type among a type's bases or interfaces now withdraws it from every rule in this batch — the same discipline `SK7080` uses for an inheritance chain it cannot walk.
